q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER WHERE PRODUCT_KEY IN (SELECT DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY FROM PRODUCT) GROUP BY CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER WHERE PRODUCT_KEY IN (SELECT DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY FROM PRODUCT) GROUP BY CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
counterexample:
INSERT INTO PRODUCT (PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1), (2), (3);
INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (101, 1), (101, 2), (101, 3), (102, 1), (102, 2);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent. Q1 groups all customers and filters those whose count of distinct product keys equals the total number of distinct products. Q2 adds an additional filter that restricts each customer to only rows where the product key exists in the product table (redundant due to foreign key, but still present). The difference arises when a customer has fewer rows than the total number of products, but Q2 may not select them if their filtered rows don't match the total count due to the WHERE clause.
counterexample_dsp: A scenario where a customer has fewer product keys than the total number of products, but after filtering in Q2, they still match the count of distinct products.
